title: Cellular therapies in non-malignant hematology
covers: What counts as cellular therapy, the three platforms (transplant, gene addition, gene editing), why fetal hemoglobin is the target, the ex vivo workflow from mobilization to engraftment, conditioning, trial endpoints, safety, long-term follow-up and the ethics of consent and access.

items.p: Cellular therapy = any treatment that uses living cells as the therapeutic agent: cells that are transplanted, expanded or selected, genetically modified, or given with a conditioning regimen.

ul: Goal: durable disease modification, sometimes after a single treatment. Supportive care manages the consequences; cellular therapy tries to restore normal biology at the source, so fewer transfusions and fewer crises.

Blood disorders begin in the stem cell, so changing the stem cell changes the whole system. HSC self-renewal keeps the pool alive; differentiation produces the myeloid lineage (red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and the lymphoid lineage (B and T cells).

table: Infuse healthy donor stem cells to replace a defective marrow (classic allogeneic HSCT)
Isolate or amplify a population (CD34+ cells, T cells) to strengthen or restore function
Add a corrective gene (gene addition) or edit a sequence (CRISPR)
Chemotherapy or radiation to make marrow space so the cells can engraft
Healthy stem cells from a donor (allogeneic) or the patient (autologous) replace a faulty blood-forming system
A viral vector (usually lentiviral) delivers a functional transgene into the patient's own HSCs
A targeted nuclease (CRISPR-Cas9) cuts at a chosen site; the cell's repair machinery rewrites the sequence or regulatory switch — no new gene is added
Required, to reduce rejection and GVHD
The correction must succeed, and conditioning is still required

items.p: These are defects of HSCs or their progeny, hereditary or acquired. Unlike cancer, the abnormal clone is not the problem — the aim is healthy production across all lineages.

ul: Hemoglobinopathies: sickle cell disease, β-thalassemia — defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival.
Inherited immunodeficiencies: SCID and related disorders — defective lymphocytes.
Marrow-failure syndromes: Fanconi anemia, aplastic anemia — too few cells of multiple lineages.
Metabolic / storage disorders: Gaucher disease, mucopolysaccharidoses — enzyme deficiencies with toxic substrate accumulation.
Red-cell and platelet disorders: selected congenital hemolytic anemias, thrombocytopenias.

table: Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into fibers; the cell becomes a rigid fragile sickle
Globin chain imbalance → ineffective erythropoiesis; precursors die in the marrow
Anemia, marrow expansion with skeletal changes, transfusion dependence
Improve the patient's own red-cell production, not just manage the anemia

summary.h: Why fetal hemoglobin is the target

ul: γ-globin is produced in fetal life and switched down after birth, when β-globin takes over; HbF is silenced in most adults.
The strategy: turn the γ-globin switch back on in the patient's own HSCs.
In sickle cell disease: HbF dilutes HbS and inhibits the polymerization that drives sickling.
In β-thalassemia: γ-globin partly replaces the missing β-globin, improving red-cell output.

One regulatory change, broad effect: editing a single control element raises HbF across the whole red-cell lineage instead of repairing each pathogenic base — an indirect correction that works whatever the mutation.

items.caption: The γ-globin switch: silenced after birth, reactivated in an edited HSC

CRISPR-Cas9 cuts at a chosen site; repair alters a sequence or regulatory element
Lyfgenia — lentiviral vector adding a modified β-globin gene for sickle cell disease

Random integration site; expression not precisely controlled
Targeted edit of a chosen element

items.p: Seven stages: mobilize → collect CD34+ → edit or transduce → release testing → condition the patient → reinfuse → monitor engraftment.

ul: Mobilization: agents such as G-CSF and plerixafor push HSCs out of the marrow niche into the blood.

Apheresis: the machine separates a CD34-enriched product and returns the remaining blood components. CD34 is a surface marker enriched on HSCs; the product is not pure (progenitors, lymphocytes, residual blood cells).
Collection gates: adequate cell dose (enough to survive manufacturing losses and still engraft), viability (dead cells cannot self-renew), sterility and traceability.
Collection is the first quality gate: a failure there cannot be rescued later — it means repeat mobilization, delay, or a product with lower engraftment potential.

items.note: Slide 14 lists G-CSF and plerixafor together as mobilizing agents. Outside the slides, G-CSF is avoided in sickle cell disease because it can precipitate severe crises; plerixafor-based mobilization is used instead. Not tested.

items.p: Activate and maintain with cytokines → deliver the edit (lentiviral vector or ribonucleoprotein complexes) → wash and formulate → cryopreserve or infuse fresh → release testing.

table: The product contains the intended CD34+ HSC population
High proportion of living cells, typically ≥ 70% post-thaw
Functional capacity to engraft and produce red cells (surrogate assays)
% of alleles modified; correlates with HbF induction potential
Leftover vector or CRISPR components below threshold

summary.h: Conditioning is part of the therapy

ul: Chemotherapy clears the hematopoietic niches and suppresses the recipient's immune system, creating marrow space so corrected HSCs can engraft. Without it, the infused cells have little room to establish durable hematopoiesis.
Toxicities: cytopenias, infection risk, mucositis, infertility, organ toxicity, hospitalization.
A perfect product does not erase conditioning risk. The patient still faces the full intensity of the regimen, which is why the decision to proceed is individualized in a non-malignant disease.

summary.h: Engraftment, lineage output and trial endpoints

items.p: Infusion → homing to the marrow niche → self-renewal → lineage output (erythroid, myeloid, megakaryocytic, lymphoid).

ul: Benefit builds slowly: mature blood cells have finite lifespans and are replaced gradually, so transfusion support and monitoring continue through the transition.

table: Hemoglobin and HbF; hemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin, reticulocytes); organ function
Transfusion independence; vaso-occlusive events; quality of life; hospitalizations
Engraftment kinetics (stem-cell take and lineage output); durability (years-long persistence)

items.note: Slide 18 scores these endpoints out of 10 in a bar chart with no explanation of where the scores come from. The endpoints are worth knowing; the numbers are not tested.

items.p: Risk depends on the whole platform — conditioning regimen, cell product and molecular strategy — not on the editing enzyme alone.

table: Conditioning causes cytopenias, mucositis, organ toxicity, hospitalization
Mild fever and chills up to anaphylactoid responses; monitor during and after reinfusion
The period before engraftment is the highest-risk window
A guide RNA may match similar sequences elsewhere → indels, deletions, translocations. Tested by in silico prediction, unbiased assays and karyotyping
Double-strand breaks → translocations and deletions beyond the cut site; p53-mediated selection shapes which cells survive
Gene addition only: integration can disrupt a gene or activate an oncogene → clonal expansion

ul: Edited HSCs self-renew for years, so monitoring must extend far beyond the infusion date: FDA guidance describes up to 15 years for certain gene-therapy products, watching for off-target edits, clonal expansion and insertional oncogenesis, and tracking durability of benefit.
"One-time administration" does not mean "one-time responsibility." Effects, intended and unintended, may appear months or years later.

Somatic, not germline. The edit is confined to the patient's blood-forming cells and is not passed to offspring; heritable germline editing is not part of approved cellular therapies, and consent must say so.
Fertility: conditioning can threaten fertility, so preservation is discussed before treatment (it adds cost and time).
Children: parents or guardians give permission; the child gives assent when developmentally appropriate. Both are documented.
Access: specialized centers, travel burden, insurance authorization, fertility-preservation cost and caregiver support decide who is actually treated. Eligibility is not purely medical.
None of the three platforms is reversible: engrafted donor cells, an integrated transgene and a genomic edit all persist.

questions.stem: Which feature makes a treatment a cellular therapy?

options.A: A viral vector is injected into the bloodstream
options.B: Living cells are the therapeutic agent
options.C: A missing protein is replaced by infusion
options.D: A cytotoxic drug clears the marrow
options.E: A monoclonal antibody blocks a surface receptor

questions.explanation: Cellular therapy encompasses any treatment that uses cells as the therapeutic agent, whether transplanted, expanded or selected, genetically modified, or combined with a conditioning regimen. A: Describes in vivo gene transfer, not a cell product. C: Protein replacement therapy. D: Conditioning chemotherapy. E: Antibody therapy.

questions.stem: What is the stated goal of cellular therapy in non-malignant hematology?

options.C: Permanent suppression of the immune system

questions.explanation: The goal is durable disease modification, sometimes after a single treatment; unlike supportive care it restores normal biology at the source. A: Supportive care, which these therapies aim to reduce. B: These diseases are not malignant. C: Immunosuppression controls GVHD, not a goal. E: These therapies aim beyond symptom control.

questions.stem: A therapy changes one control element in the genome of a patient's stem cells without inserting a new gene. Which strategy is this?

options.A: A regulatory switch is rewritten at a chosen site
options.B: A functional transgene is inserted into the genome
options.C: A lentiviral vector carries a new gene copy
options.D: Donor stem cells replace the marrow compartment
options.E: Collected T cells are amplified in culture

questions.explanation: Gene editing uses targeted nucleases to rewrite a selected genomic sequence or regulatory switch, with no whole new gene added. B: Gene addition. C: Gene addition. D: Transplantation. E: Expansion and selection.

questions.stem: Which property of hematopoietic stem cells makes a single administration potentially durable?
questions.explanation: HSC self-renewal keeps the stem-cell pool alive, so edited or transplanted HSCs persist and keep producing blood cells for years. A: Produces mature cells that die and are replaced. B: Mobilization moves them there for collection. D: A silencer of γ-globin, not a durability mechanism. E: Stem cells do not become the niche.

questions.stem: From which lineage do monocytes and macrophages arise?
questions.explanation: Myeloid pathway: red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages. Lymphoid pathway: B cells and T cells. A: B and T cells. B: Marrow microenvironment. C: Vessel lining. D: Connective tissue.

questions.stem: A laboratory isolates CD34+ cells from a collection and amplifies them in culture. Which cellular therapy strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Expand or select: isolate or amplify specific cell populations such as CD34+ cells or T cells to strengthen or restore function. A: Supplies a transgene with a vector. B: Rewrites a genomic sequence. C: Creates marrow space before infusion. E: Uses donor stem cells.

questions.stem: A collected stem-cell product goes straight to infusion with no laboratory manufacturing step. Which platform is this?
questions.explanation: In the comparison table, HSC transplantation involves no manufacturing (cells are collected fresh); only graft processing is done. A: Ex vivo transduction and complex release testing. B: Ex vivo editing with guide RNA and Cas9. D: Culture in the laboratory. E: Manufactured before reinfusion.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia will receive his own hematopoietic stem cells after laboratory editing. Which complication does this avoid?
questions.explanation: Autologous cells eliminate donor matching and GVHD; the patient receives his own edited cells, with no allogeneic immune response. B: Conditioning is still given. C: Can follow any cell product. D: A conditioning toxicity. E: A risk of the editing platform.

questions.stem: After allogeneic transplantation a patient takes long-term drugs that autologous platforms do not require. Which drugs?
questions.explanation: Long-term immunosuppressive drugs are often needed after allogeneic transplant to control graft-versus-host disease. A: Treat iron overload. C: Used before collection. D: Control bleeding. E: Support cells in culture.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease has no suitable HLA-matched donor. Which platform avoids the donor requirement?
questions.explanation: Gene addition and CRISPR editing both use autologous cells, so no donor is needed; HSC transplantation requires a matched related or unrelated donor. A: Needs a donor. B: Needs a donor. C: Needs a donor. D: Needs a donor.

questions.stem: How do the non-malignant targets of cellular therapy differ from leukemia?

options.A: The abnormal clone is not the problem
options.B: The hematopoietic stem cell is unaffected
options.C: The marrow is replaced by fibrosis

questions.explanation: These disorders arise from defects in HSCs or their progeny; unlike cancer the abnormal clone is not the problem, and the goal is to restore healthy blood-cell production across all lineages. B: Defects lie in HSCs or their progeny. C: Not the described mechanism. D: Conditioning is still required. E: Allogeneic transplant is one option.

questions.stem: Which disease group is targeted because defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia) are listed as targets because defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival. A: Defective lymphocytes. B: Insufficient production of several lineages. C: Enzyme deficiencies with substrate accumulation. D: A platelet lineage defect.

questions.stem: An infant with severe combined immunodeficiency is referred for cellular therapy. Which lineage is defective?
questions.explanation: Inherited immunodeficiencies such as SCID are listed among the targets: defective lymphocytes fail to mount immune responses. A: Red cell production. C: Platelet production. D: Granulocytes and monocytes. E: The marrow niche.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with short stature, absent thumbs and pancytopenia is assessed for cellular therapy. Which marrow-failure syndrome is this?
questions.explanation: Marrow-failure syndromes listed are Fanconi anemia and aplastic anemia: the marrow cannot produce sufficient blood cells of multiple lineages. A: No congenital anomalies. B: Metabolic and storage disorder. D: Hemoglobinopathy. E: Inherited immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A toddler has an enzyme deficiency that lets toxic substrate build up in his tissues. Which listed target is this?
questions.explanation: Metabolic and storage disorders such as Gaucher disease and the mucopolysaccharidoses are enzyme deficiencies that accumulate toxic substrates in tissues. A: Marrow failure. B: Hemoglobinopathy. C: Marrow failure. E: Immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A boy with sickle cell disease develops an ischemic pain crisis after a night of hypoxia. Which molecular event begins the cascade?

options.B: Loss of spectrin from the red cell membrane
options.D: Complement deposition on the red cell
options.E: Antibody binding to the red cell surface

questions.explanation: When HbS gives up oxygen the molecules stack into long fibers; the fibers bend the erythrocyte into a rigid fragile sickle, causing hemolysis and vaso-occlusion. A: Not the sickling mechanism. B: Hereditary spherocytosis. D: Immune hemolysis. E: Immune hemolysis.

questions.stem: A child with β-thalassemia major has a hypercellular marrow, severe anemia and a low reticulocyte count. What drives this ineffective erythropoiesis?

options.B: Loss of the CD34 surface marker
options.C: Failure of the γ-globin switch at birth

questions.explanation: Reduced or absent β-globin impairs hemoglobin assembly; the globin chain imbalance triggers ineffective erythropoiesis, so precursors die in the marrow. B: A stem-cell marker, not a cause. C: Persistent HbF would help, not harm. D: Not the described mechanism. E: Affects surviving circulating cells.

questions.stem: A child with untreated β-thalassemia has frontal bossing and widened facial bones. Which process explains these skeletal changes?
questions.explanation: Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and skeletal changes, alongside chronic anemia and growth delay. A: A sickle cell complication. B: Infection. C: Not a described effect. D: Not the described mechanism.

questions.stem: Which gene product takes over from γ-globin after birth?
questions.explanation: During fetal life γ-globin chains are produced; after birth the β-globin gene takes over and this developmental switch silences HbF in most adults. A: Expressed before and after birth. C: A minor adult chain, not the switch partner. D: Embryonic. E: Embryonic.

questions.stem: After therapy a boy with sickle cell disease has an HbF of 35% and no further pain crises. Which change explains the benefit?

options.A: HbF corrects the β-globin point mutation
options.B: HbF displaces HbS from the red cell
options.E: HbF blocks iron loading of the red cell

questions.explanation: Increased HbF levels dilute hemoglobin S and inhibit the polymerization that drives sickling and vaso-occlusion. A: Reactivating HbF repairs no DNA base. B: HbS remains in the cell. C: No conversion occurs. E: Unrelated to sickling.

questions.stem: Two patients with different β-globin mutations both improve after the same BCL11A-targeted therapy. Why does one edit work for both?

options.A: It repairs each pathogenic base in the β-globin gene
options.B: It replaces the entire β-globin locus
options.C: It silences the mutant β-globin allele
options.E: It raises HbF across the red-cell lineage

questions.explanation: One regulatory change has a broad effect: editing a single control element can raise HbF across the entire red-cell lineage rather than repairing each pathogenic mutation. A: Base-by-base repair is what this strategy avoids. B: No locus replacement occurs. C: Silencing the mutant allele is not the mechanism. D: Gene addition, a different platform.

questions.stem: Lyfgenia delivers a modified β-globin gene into a patient's own stem cells with a lentiviral vector. Which long-term risk belongs to this platform?

options.B: Off-target cleavage by a guide RNA

questions.explanation: For gene-addition platforms, vector integration can disrupt endogenous genes or activate an oncogene, leading to clonal expansion or insertional oncogenesis. A: The cells are autologous. B: Editing platforms. D: Follows double-strand breaks in editing. E: No donor is involved.

questions.stem: A product reactivates fetal hemoglobin by editing the BCL11A erythroid enhancer. Which product is it?
questions.explanation: Casgevy edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin production; Lyfgenia is the gene-addition example. A: Adds a modified β-globin gene with a lentiviral vector. C: An iron chelator. D: A complement inhibitor. E: A mobilizing agent.

questions.stem: In the ex vivo workflow, which step immediately follows quality-control release testing?
questions.explanation: The seven stages run: mobilize, collect CD34+ cells, edit or transduce, release testing, condition the patient, reinfuse, monitor engraftment. B: Stage 2. C: Stage 3. D: Stage 6, after conditioning. E: Stage 1.

questions.stem: Before collection a patient is given a drug for several days and his circulating CD34+ count rises sharply. Which drug was given?
questions.explanation: Mobilizing agents such as G-CSF and plerixafor push HSCs out of the marrow niche into the bloodstream, increasing the circulating stem cells available for collection. A: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist. B: An anti-CD20 antibody. C: An iron chelator. E: A corticosteroid.

questions.stem: During apheresis for a gene therapy, what does the machine give back to the patient?
questions.explanation: Apheresis draws blood, separates the CD34+ cells and returns the remaining blood components to the patient, yielding a concentrated stem-cell product. A: That is kept for manufacturing. C: A drug given beforehand. D: Used later in the laboratory. E: Given after manufacturing.

questions.stem: What does the CD34 marker identify in the collected product?
questions.explanation: CD34 is a surface marker enriched on human HSCs; the goal is a product with enough viable CD34+ cells to reconstitute all blood lineages. A: Not the enriched population. B: There is no donor in an autologous product. D: Niche cells, not collected. E: Not the marker's target.

questions.stem: Besides stem cells and progenitors, what else does the apheresis product contain?
questions.explanation: The apheresis product is not a pure stem-cell suspension: it also contains progenitor cells, lymphocytes and residual blood cells. B: Remain in the niche. C: Remain in the bone. D: Not in blood. E: Added later in the laboratory.

questions.stem: A cell product is recalled and the team must show which patient it came from and every step it passed through. Which collection parameter allows this?
questions.explanation: Traceability is a chain of identity linking each product to the patient and every manufacturing step, protecting safety and quality control. A: Functional capacity to engraft. B: Confirms the intended cell population. C: Absence of microbial contamination. E: Proportion of living cells.

questions.stem: Why must a generous number of CD34+ cells be collected rather than the minimum?

options.A: Editing efficiency falls with fewer cells
options.B: Conditioning works less well with fewer cells
options.C: Viability improves with a larger dose
options.D: Sterility testing consumes most of the product

questions.explanation: Enough CD34+ cells must be collected to survive manufacturing losses and still engraft after conditioning. A: Efficiency is a per-allele measure. B: Conditioning acts on the recipient. C: Viability reflects cell health. D: Testing uses a small sample.

questions.stem: Apheresis yields fewer viable CD34+ cells than the manufacturing target requires. What follows?

options.E: A second round of release testing

questions.explanation: Collection is the first quality gate; a poor collection means the patient may need repeat mobilization, face delays, or receive a product with lower engraftment potential. A: Does not replace a low cell dose. B: A laboratory measure cannot supply missing cells. D: A formulation choice. E: Tests the product, does not enlarge it.

options.B: Failures there cannot be rescued later
options.E: It confirms sterility of the final product

questions.explanation: Collection is the first quality gate in the ex vivo workflow: failures there cannot be rescued later in manufacturing. A: Autologous products need no matching. C: A separate clinical decision. D: Determined in the laboratory. E: Release testing does that.

questions.explanation: Cells are activated and maintained in culture with cytokines to support survival and proliferation before the edit is delivered. B: Used to condition the patient. C: An immunosuppressant. D: Not part of manufacturing. E: Not used to activate cells.

questions.stem: In what form are CRISPR components usually delivered to the cells in the laboratory?
questions.explanation: The edit is delivered either by a lentiviral vector or by ribonucleoprotein complexes. A: Used for gene addition. B: Not the described route. C: Not a delivery method here. D: A drug formulation.

questions.stem: Release testing of a manufactured cell product checks each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Release testing covers identity, viability, sterility, potency, editing efficiency and residual reagent. HLA typing belongs to allogeneic transplantation, where a donor must be matched. A: Confirms the intended CD34+ population. B: Excludes bacteria, fungi and mycoplasma. C: Functional capacity to engraft. E: Proportion of living cells.

questions.stem: A thawed cell product contains 62% living cells. Which release specification does it fail?
questions.explanation: Viability: a high proportion of living cells, typically ≥ 70% post-thaw. A: Measures modified alleles. B: Measures leftover components. C: Excludes contamination. D: Measures engraftment capacity.

questions.stem: Which release test measures the product's functional capacity to engraft and produce red cells?

questions.explanation: Residual reagent testing checks for leftover vector or CRISPR components below a threshold before release. B: Measures engraftment capacity. C: Confirms the cell population. D: Detects microbial growth. E: Measures living cells.

questions.stem: Why is chemotherapy given before corrected stem cells are reinfused?

questions.explanation: Recognized conditioning toxicities are cytopenias, infection risk, mucositis, infertility, organ toxicity and hospitalization. A: A molecular risk of editing. B: A vector-related risk. C: A vector-related risk. D: Follows double-strand breaks.

questions.explanation: Hemolysis markers followed in trials are LDH, bilirubin and reticulocytes. A: Stem-cell take and lineage output. B: Freedom from transfusion. D: End-organ damage. E: Impact on daily living.

questions.explanation: Engraftment kinetics describe stem-cell take and lineage output; they are a key outcome in trials and clinical follow-up. A: Years-long persistence of benefit. B: A product release test. C: A laboratory measure of the product. E: Avoids silent end-organ damage.

questions.explanation: Durability is listed as the endpoint for years-long persistence of benefit. A: Early stem-cell take. B: Measured before release. D: Measured before release. E: Healthcare utilization.

questions.stem: Which part of a gene-editing platform produces the acute cytopenias and mucositis seen after treatment?
questions.explanation: Risk depends on the entire platform, not the editing enzyme alone: chemotherapy-based conditioning causes cytopenias, mucositis, organ toxicity and hospitalization. A: Determines where the nuclease cuts. B: Makes the targeted DNA break. C: Preserves the product. D: Collects the cells.

questions.stem: During reinfusion of the manufactured product a patient develops fever and chills. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Reinfusing the manufactured product can trigger infusion-related reactions, from mild fever and chills to anaphylactoid responses. B: The cells are autologous. C: A molecular event with no acute fever. D: Becomes apparent weeks later. E: A late clonal complication.

questions.stem: When is the risk of serious infection highest in a patient receiving autologous gene therapy?
questions.explanation: Conditioning-induced cytopenias create a window of vulnerability; the period before engraftment is the highest-risk window. A: Counts are not yet suppressed. C: A collection procedure. D: Counts have recovered. E: Counts have recovered.

questions.stem: Sequencing after CRISPR therapy finds small indels at a site unrelated to the intended target. What caused them?

options.A: A vector integrates beside an oncogene
options.B: The transgene is silenced after integration
options.D: A guide RNA matches a similar sequence
options.E: The product thaws with low viability

questions.explanation: A guide RNA may recognize similar DNA sequences beyond the intended site; double-strand breaks there create small indels, larger deletions or translocations. A: Gene addition. B: An expression problem. C: A toxicity. E: A manufacturing issue.

questions.stem: Which method is used to look for off-target editing?
questions.explanation: Off-target testing combines in silico prediction, unbiased assays and karyotyping. A: Measures living cells. B: Detects contamination. C: Matches donors. D: Assesses iron status.

questions.stem: A double-strand break extends beyond the intended cut site. Which genomic change can result?

options.B: A point mutation in a promoter

questions.explanation: Double-strand breaks can produce chromosomal rearrangements including translocations and deletions that extend beyond the cut site. B: Not a consequence of a double-strand break here. C: Belongs to gene addition. D: A manufacturing issue. E: A collection issue.

questions.stem: Which protein may shape which edited cells survive after double-strand breaks are made?
questions.explanation: Double-strand breaks can drive p53-mediated selection, shaping which cells survive; long-term monitoring is required to detect clonal evolution. A: The transcription factor that silences γ-globin. B: The nuclease making the break. D: A stem-cell surface marker. E: A red cell membrane protein.

questions.stem: How can a lentiviral vector cause clonal expansion years after treatment?
questions.explanation: Vector integration can disrupt endogenous genes or activate oncogenes, leading to clonal expansion or insertional oncogenesis. A: An editing platform does that. C: Follows double-strand breaks. D: Conditioning does that. E: A manufacturing issue.

questions.stem: Which feature separates gene addition from gene editing?
questions.explanation: Gene addition adds a transgene at a random integration site with gene expression not precisely controlled; CRISPR makes a targeted edit, for example at the BCL11A enhancer. A: True of both platforms. B: True of both platforms. C: True of both platforms. E: True of both platforms.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by transplantation, gene addition and gene editing?

options.D: They repair the β-globin point mutation

questions.explanation: Reversibility: engrafted donor cells, an integrated transgene and a genomic edit all persist, so none of the three platforms is reversible. B: All three require conditioning. C: Only transplantation does. D: None repairs the mutation itself. E: Each carries its own uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which platform requires quality control for editing efficiency?
questions.explanation: In the comparison table, CRISPR editing involves ex vivo editing with guide RNA and Cas9 delivery plus QC for editing efficiency. A: No genetic alteration is made. C: Release testing checks transduction, not editing. D: Supportive care. E: Supportive care.

questions.stem: For how long does FDA guidance describe extended monitoring of certain gene-therapy products?
questions.explanation: FDA guidance describes extended monitoring up to 15 years for certain human gene-therapy products. A: Shorter than the guidance. B: Shorter than the guidance. C: Shorter than the guidance. E: Longer than the guidance.

questions.stem: Why must follow-up continue for years after a single infusion of edited stem cells?

options.A: The conditioning drug has a long half-life
options.B: The vector keeps replicating in the blood
options.C: The change is passed to the patient's offspring
options.E: The edited cells self-renew for years

questions.explanation: Gene and cell therapies persist because the edited HSC compartment self-renews and keeps producing blood cells across the patient's lifetime. A: Its effects are acute. B: It does not replicate. C: The therapy is somatic. D: The aim is transfusion independence.

questions.stem: Which delayed adverse events does long-term surveillance after gene therapy look for?
questions.explanation: Surveillance is for delayed adverse events: off-target edits, clonal expansion and vector-related insertional oncogenesis, alongside tracking of durability. A: An acute event. B: An acute conditioning toxicity. D: Occurs before engraftment. E: An acute event.

questions.stem: A family lives far from the few hospitals offering gene therapy. Which access barrier does this describe?
questions.explanation: Collection, manufacturing and transplant expertise is concentrated at a limited number of sites, and patients may need repeated long-distance trips for evaluation, apheresis and follow-up. A: A product problem. B: A product problem. C: Applies to donor transplants. E: A product problem.

questions.stem: A young woman is offered fertility preservation before gene therapy. What is the reason?
questions.explanation: Conditioning can threaten fertility, so fertility preservation must be discussed before treatment; it adds cost and time. B: The therapy is somatic. C: Not a described risk. D: A blood collection procedure. E: Not a described effect.

questions.stem: A teenager asks whether the therapy will change the genes she passes to her children. Which feature of the therapy answers her question?

options.A: It is delivered by a lentiviral vector
options.C: It uses a guide RNA of high specificity
options.E: It is monitored for up to 15 years

questions.explanation: Somatic editing targets the patient's own blood cells and the changes are not passed to offspring; heritable germline editing is not part of current approved cellular therapies. A: Describes the platform, not heritability. C: Precision concerns off-target sites. D: Unrelated to heritability. E: Describes follow-up, not heritability.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old is enrolled for gene therapy. What does the child provide in addition to parental permission?
questions.explanation: Children cannot give full legal consent: parents or guardians provide permission and the child's assent is sought when developmentally appropriate, both documented. A: Children cannot give it. B: A legal instrument for adults. D: Given on another's behalf. E: Follow-up is part of the therapy.

questions.stem: Why does a single administration not mean a single episode of responsibility?

options.A: The infusion is repeated each year
options.B: Conditioning is given a second time
options.E: Effects may appear years after treatment

questions.explanation: Because edited HSCs last for years, intended and unintended effects may only become visible months or years after treatment, so long-term follow-up is an ethical commitment. A: It is given once. B: It precedes the one infusion. C: The aim is transfusion independence. D: No re-dosing is described.

questions.stem: Which question comes first when reasoning through a cellular therapy decision?

options.C: Whether the cells are autologous or allogeneic

questions.explanation: The checklist starts by identifying the defective lineage — erythroid, myeloid, lymphoid progenitors or the hematopoietic stem cell itself — before choosing a strategy. A: Step 4. C: Step 3. D: Step 5. E: Step 6.
